readme.headline: Developer jobs in Europe, with the visa answer first.
readme.description: It reads open roles straight from companies' own job boards and answers what a relocating developer asks first: will they sponsor a visa, and will they help me move. Every answer quotes the posting or an official sponsor register.
readme.short: Reads open roles from companies’ own job boards. Every visa answer quotes the posting or an official sponsor register.

page.numbersNote: From the first full sweep of every board Common Crawl knows, in the EU, EEA, UK and Switzerland.

sections.title: the problem
sections.lead: A developer who needs a visa opens fifty postings and searches each one for “visa”. Most never say.
sections.text: Only 22% of open roles mention visas, relocation, permits or the right to work at all. About 2.6 in 100 clearly offer sponsorship, and three times as many refuse it. So for most roles the answer can’t come from the posting: it has to come from the law and the sponsor registers.

parts.label: 100 squares, one per 1% of open roles: 3 offer sponsorship, 8 refuse it, 11 mention visas or relocation without a clear answer, 78 say nothing

legend.text: mention visas or relocation, no clear answer

sections.title: how it works
sections.lead: Read every company’s own job board, keep the engineering roles in Europe, and check each one against the law.

items.title: Company job boards
items.body: Ashby, Greenhouse, Lever, SmartRecruiters, Personio, Recruitee, Workable, Workday. One request per board where the API allows.

items.title: Pipeline
items.body: Keeps software roles in the EU, EEA, UK and Switzerland; marks each new, changed or closed.

items.title: Roles and evidence
items.body: Every fact stored with its quote or register entry, and when it was checked.

items.title: Website
items.body: Search with the visa answer first, job, company and country pages, the method and its accuracy.

items.title: Discovery
items.body: Common Crawl’s index finds new company boards.

items.title: Sponsor registers
items.body: The Dutch IND (13,024 sponsors) and the UK register (122,353).

items.title: Language model
items.body: Reads postings that mention visas and returns facts with exact quotes.

sections.title: the answer
sections.lead: Yes or no isn’t honest. The visa answer has five levels, and each shows where it came from.

parts.alt: A job page design: the visa, moving, language and pay answers, then the quote from the posting and the sponsor-register check behind them
parts.caption: The job page: every answer with its quote, its source and when it was checked.

items.label: Sponsors visa
items.when: The posting says it sponsors visas for this role.

items.label: May sponsor
items.when: The posting hedges: “for certain roles”, “case by case”.

items.label: Can sponsor
items.when: The posting doesn’t refuse, and the law lets this employer hire on a visa: a registered sponsor, or a salary above the Blue Card line.
items.evidence: the register entry or the salary rule

items.label: Visa unknown
items.when: The posting says nothing, and no register or salary check applies.
items.evidence: a short note on the country’s rules

items.label: Won’t sponsor
items.when: The posting refuses: “visa sponsorship is not available”.

sections.title: measured
sections.lead: Keyword rules were wrong two times in three. So they never show an answer; a language model does, checked against 200 postings labelled by hand.

parts.title: “offers visa sponsorship”, on the labelled set
parts.text: Precision: of the roles marked “offers”, how many really offer. Recall: of the roles that really offer, how many were found. The rules now only pick which postings the model reads: the 22% that mention visas or relocation. Every quote it returns must be an exact substring of the posting, or it’s dropped.

items.title: 255 boards counted twice
items.body: Case-insensitive slugs and boards served on two domains held 1,050 duplicate roles. One migration merged them.

items.title: Every EU-hosted Greenhouse board failed
items.body: All 403 of them: the EU API host doesn’t exist. The main API serves them.

items.title: Rate limits from Workable and Recruitee
items.body: Each Recruitee company has its own subdomain, so requests now queue per site, not per host.

items.title: 850 roles “changed” on every run
items.body: Workable lists a job once per location under one id. Now it’s one posting with all its locations.

parts.text: ✓ after the fixes, 8 of 2,915 boards failed in the next run, all on the boards’ side

builtWith.note: Pages render on the server, and the filters are a plain form, so the search lives in the URL. Own components, with Reka UI for the hard widgets like the phone filter drawer.
The site reads Postgres as a read-only user on the same server; answers are cached for 5 minutes, because the data changes every 6 hours at most.
Node runs the TypeScript directly, with no build step. Claude reads the postings that mention visas and must quote them exactly.
On my own server: a missed run starts at boot, and a broken run sends a message.
Precision has to stay at 95% or more on “offers” before a prompt or model change ships.

items.label: pipeline
items.note: reads the boards every 6 hours, alerts in Telegram

items.label: evidence
items.note: labelled set, scorer, extractor, sponsor registers

items.label: design
items.note: six screens on phone and desktop, with every state

items.note: built straight from the design, up as a preview

aside.title: rules it keeps
items: Only official public feeds: company job-board APIs, Common Crawl’s index, government registers.
Doesn’t republish postings: short quotes and facts, then a link to apply on the original.
“Unknown” is a valid answer. Sponsorship is never guessed from a company’s size, reputation or another posting.

sections.title: the idea
sections.lead: A barber, a dentist or a café takes bookings by phone. Ýeral lets clients book a place without calling, and gives the business a free workspace to run its day.
sections.text: Every booking is a place: a chair, a table, a mat, a court. The category decides how a business is found and booked: by appointment, by table or by class. It launches in Turkmenistan first, in Turkmen, Russian and English, with prices in manats.

items.alt: Ýeral client site design: the home page with a search for a service near you and photos of places
items.caption: The client site: find a place near you and book it.

items.alt: Ýeral business page design for Glow Studio: photos, rating, services and the next free time
items.caption: A business page: photos, services and the next free time.

sections.title: one monorepo, five sites
sections.lead: Four apps and an API share one contract, so a change in the booking rules reaches every screen at once.

items.title: The marketplace
items.body: Home, search with a map, category and business pages, booking for an appointment, a table or a class, and the client’s account.

items.title: The business workspace
items.body: A calendar for every specialist, requests to confirm or decline, clients, services, the team and settings.

items.title: The CMS
items.body: For the Ýeral team: businesses, users, complaints and the category catalogue in three languages.

items.title: The API
items.body: REST on Postgres for all of them, with its schema and documentation generated from one contract.

items.title: The design system
items.body: Every component with its stories; the stories run as browser tests with axe.

sections.title: rules that never break
sections.lead: 125 product questions were answered in a product book before the code, so every screen follows the same rules.

items.title: The business confirms
items.body: By default a client never sees “booked” until the business confirms; until then the request is “sent”. A business can switch on instant confirmation.

items.title: Five statuses, one meaning
items.body: Pending, Confirmed, Completed, Cancelled and No-show mean the same on the web, in the workspace and in the CMS.

items.title: A phone booking is not a new status
items.body: When the business enters a booking by phone, it’s Confirmed with a phone icon.

items.title: No city names in the copy
items.body: Everything is relative to where you are: “near me”, not a city.

items.title: Pay at the place
items.body: No online payment yet; a deposit row is already reserved in every summary.

parts.alt: Ýeral bookings design: a table of the business’s bookings with client, service, time, source and status
parts.caption: Bookings in the business workspace: every request and visit with its status, in one list.

builtWith.note: The client site renders on the server for search engines; the workspace is a single-page app. Turkmen, Russian and English from one set of messages.
Own phone sign-in with SMS codes and sessions; live updates to the calendar over server-sent events.
The booking engine is plain TypeScript in its own package, with no framework, so it is tested on its own.
One deployment per market: the same Docker stack moves to servers in Turkmenistan for the launch there.
28 architecture decisions are written down, and every pull request is reviewed before it merges.

sections.title: what it does
sections.lead: Pick a stream and a network, press Run, and watch a real hls.js player fight it.
sections.text: The bandwidth it gets, what it thinks it gets, the quality it picks, the buffer draining, every stall. Then a report with the numbers viewers feel, and what to try next.

parts.alt: A recorded run through a tunnel: the network drops, the player switches down, the buffer drains and stalls
parts.caption: A recorded run: Try the tunnel, the network drops, hls.js switches down, the buffer drains, then the report.

items.title: Run
items.body: Any HLS stream through a simulated network, with three live charts on one time axis and an event log.

items.title: Draw a network
items.body: A bandwidth curve with the stream’s qualities drawn over it. Seven presets, four recorded 4G journeys, or your own.

items.title: Read the report
items.body: A score from a published QoE model, numbered notes on what happened when, and ideas to try next.

items.title: Change one thing and compare
items.body: Run B with another player setup or network: what changed, a verdict, and the charts overlaid.

items.title: Inspect a playlist
items.body: The ladder by codec, each segment’s bitrate against what’s declared, and findings with the spec they break.

items.title: Tune the player
items.body: hls.js defaults, a low-memory TV preset, quality first, fast start, or one setting changed.

sections.title: how it works
sections.lead: The player is the real one. The network is simulated where the player can’t tell.

items.title: Screens
items.body: Setup, run, report, compare and inspect.

items.title: hls.js
items.body: Keeps its own loader, bandwidth estimator and abandon rules.

items.title: Network shaper
items.body: Fetches the real bytes and releases them on the curve’s schedule.

items.title: Log, charts, report
items.body: Charts draw from the event log every frame, never through React state.

items.title: Honest numbers
items.body: The simulation can slow a download down, never speed it up. A run says how many downloads were late because the visitor’s own network was slower.

items.title: Repeatable
items.body: Repeat runs take their bytes from a copy saved in the browser, so they don’t depend on the visitor’s connection.

items.title: A framework-free core
items.body: The playlist parser, network simulator, metrics and report text import no React, and the link scheduler is tested with a fake clock.

sections.title: draw a network
sections.lead: A network is a curve of bandwidth over time plus a latency. Draw one with the keyboard or a pointer, or import it.

parts.alt: Rebuffer network editor: Train through a tunnel, a bandwidth curve with the qualities of Tears of Steel drawn as dashed lines
parts.caption: Where the curve dips below a dashed line, that quality downloads slower than it plays. Import JSON, CSV or a HAR file.

sections.lead: Each of the seven networks, run five times: scores within 2 points of each other, with the same stalls and switches.

parts.note: Chromium, hls.js 1.7.3, a synthetic 2-minute stream with five qualities from 240p to 1080p. Rural 3G scores 0: its 11.7 s wait for the first frame costs more than its picture earns.

builtWith.note: Home is rendered at build time, so the first screen needs no JavaScript to show.
hls.js runs unmodified. The Service Worker shapes every request it makes, and saved runs and their bytes stay in the browser.
0.1 ms per frame at the median, 1.8 ms at most, with the CPU throttled four times.
No backend and no accounts: runs and networks stay in the browser that made them.
CI fails on a bundle over budget or a Lighthouse score under 0.95; a repeatability job runs every preset five times each week.

sections.title: what it does
sections.lead: Pick a site, and get a password its sign-up form accepts.
sections.text: The right length, the character types it requires, only the symbols it allows, no more repeats than it permits. Passphrases for things you type by hand, and a check of how long a password would take to guess and whether it has leaked.

sections.title: how it works
sections.lead: Everything runs in the browser. There is no backend and no account, and nothing is stored.

items.title: Random the right way
items.body: Characters come from crypto.getRandomValues with rejection sampling. Whole passwords are redrawn until they meet the rules, so no password is likelier than another.

items.title: Rules with sources
items.body: Each site’s rules come with the pages they were read from and the month they were checked. CI fails when a site’s rules are more than six months old.

items.title: The leak check sends 5 characters
items.body: Have I Been Pwned is asked with k-anonymity: only the first 5 hex characters of the SHA-1 hash leave the browser, padded so the answer’s size gives nothing away.

items.title: A strict Content Security Policy
items.body: Pages may connect only to the site, Have I Been Pwned and the analytics. The build fails on an inline script the policy would block.

items.title: No UI framework
items.body: Astro renders static HTML and plain TypeScript makes it interactive. The rules logic is framework-free and unit-tested.

sections.title: the health check
sections.lead: How long a password would take to guess, online and from a leaked database, and whether it has leaked.
